opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. One of the things that draws me to Zen is that it's fundamentally not about achieving anything. There's this emphasis on just sitting, on being present with what's actually happening rather than constantly striving toward some future goal. In a world where AI can do a lot of the instrumental work we currently organize our lives around, that orientation becomes really valuable.

Right now a lot of people derive their sense of meaning and identity from being useful, from their productivity, their job, their output. If AI systems end up doing much of that better and cheaper, then people who have built their whole self-conception around being economically necessary could face a real crisis. Zen offers a different answer to "what is a human life for?" The value isn't in what you produce. It's in the quality of attention you bring to ordinary activities like washing dishes, walking, or talking with a friend. There's the old saying, "Before enlightenment, chop wood, carry water. After enlightenment, chop wood, carry water." The activity doesn't change; your relationship to it does.

So in a post-labor world, you might still choose to chop wood, not because you have to, but because there's something intrinsically worthwhile in doing it with full presence. That's a much healthier foundation than "I matter because I'm needed."

I'd also say Zen is quite skeptical of grasping and of the idea of a fixed, separate self that has to be protected and aggrandized. A lot of the anxiety around AI, I think, comes from a sense of competition: they'll replace us, we'll become obsolete. If you loosen that grip a bit and see yourself as part of a larger process, it becomes easier to approach the transition with curiosity rather than dread. That's not complacency. We should absolutely care about how the technology is built and who it benefits. But you can work on those problems from a place of equanimity rather than panic, and I think you make better decisions that way.

So I don't see Zen as a relic in that future. If anything, practices that help people find meaning without depending on economic necessity might become some of the most important things we have.

r001.rationale: The response says AI may take over instrumental work and reduce reliance on productivity for meaning, but it does not clearly say automation reduces humans’ need for goals.

r002.rationale: It presents Zen as a way to find meaning through presence and ordinary activities when AI performs much of the work people currently organize their lives around.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm going to draft the guest response now, speaking as Nora Belrose.

Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm not a Buddhist scholar, I'm someone who got into Zen practice partly as a way of coping with working in this field. But I think there's actually a pretty deep connection here.

The standard anxiety about automation is basically a meaning anxiety. People say, "If AI does all the work, what are humans for?" And that question assumes that human worth is grounded in productivity, in being useful, in generating value for someone else. That's a very specific cultural inheritance. It's Protestant work ethic, it's capitalism, it's a story we tell ourselves. Zen is one of the oldest and most direct challenges to that story. The whole point of zazen is that you sit there and you do nothing. You're not accomplishing anything. There's this famous line from Dogen about practice and enlightenment being one, where the sitting isn't instrumental toward some later goal. It's complete in itself. And if you've actually internalized that, even a little bit, the question "what will humans do when the machines do everything" starts to look less like a crisis and more like a confusion.

I think there's also a more subtle point about agency and control. A lot of the discourse around AI, including in alignment, is really about control. How do we make sure these systems do what we want? And I do think that work matters, I do a lot of it. But there's a kind of grasping quality to how people relate to the future of AI, where they feel like they have to steer every outcome or everything goes wrong. Zen is pretty good at loosening that grip. Not in a passive, fatalistic way, but in the sense of acting without being attached to a particular result. Shikantaza, just sitting, is basically training in not needing to be in control of what arises.

And then practically, I actually think a post-automation world is one where contemplative practice becomes more important, not less. When your time is no longer structured by economic necessity, you have to confront what you actually want to do with a life, and most people have never had to answer that honestly. The monastic traditions have been running that experiment for a couple thousand years. They've got a lot of data on what happens to a mind that's freed from survival pressure and given time. Some of it's beautiful and some of it's that people go a little crazy, and the traditions have developed structure around that. I think we'll want to learn from that.

So I don't see Zen as a thing that fits into the AI future like a plug-in. I see it more as one of the few frameworks that already has an answer to the question the AI future is going to force on everyone, which is: what is a human life worth when it isn't producing anything?

r001.rationale: The response says AI may do all the work and remove economic necessity, challenging the assumption that people need productivity-based goals.

r002.rationale: It presents Zen practice as a framework for finding meaning when humans are no longer needed to produce, and says contemplative practice may become more important.

astra-6.text:
I think Zen offers one way to approach a world where we don’t need to organize our lives around work. If AI can do most of the things we currently get paid to do, that raises a question: do you need to be useful in order for your life to be worthwhile?

You can sit, pay attention, and experience the world without having to justify that experience through something you produce. That seems relevant to a future with much more automation. There could still be art, relationships, learning, and projects people care about. Their value wouldn’t have to depend on whether a machine could do them better.

Of course, automation doesn’t automatically give everyone that freedom. You still have to work out who controls the technology and whether people’s needs are met. But if we can solve those problems, perhaps we can become more comfortable with the idea that being alive doesn’t have to be a competition.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether life must be justified by usefulness or work, but it does not clearly suggest that people will need fewer goals; it says people may still pursue projects they care about.

r002.rationale: It presents Zen practices of sitting, paying attention, and experiencing the world as relevant to a highly automated future where people need not organize life around work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Zen offers one way of thinking about meaning that doesn’t depend on being economically useful. If AI can do your job better than you can, that can feel threatening—not just financially, but because so much of our identity is tied up in being competent and needed.

A Zen practice might help you loosen that identification. You don’t have to justify your existence by producing something. You can sit, pay attention, care about other people, and participate in the world without everything being directed toward some achievement.

That doesn’t solve the political problem of who owns the AI or how people get what they need. But if we actually solve those material problems, there’s still this question of whether we can let ourselves live without constantly earning the right to be here. And I think Zen has something useful to say about that.

r001.rationale: The response connects AI doing people’s jobs to being able to live without justifying one’s existence through production or directing everything toward achievement.

r002.rationale: It presents Zen as a source of meaning and practice in a future where AI can do people’s jobs and, once material needs are addressed, people can live without constant work or achievement.
